title: Python
blurb: The foundation everything else is built on — syntax through advanced features.

lessons.title: Aptech Beginner 1 — Python environment, execution & foundations
lessons.explanation: Before syntax becomes useful, you need a reliable workflow: know which Python version is running, how a .py file is executed, how the command line and editor fit together, how environment variables affect programs, and how help() and dir() let you inspect unfamiliar objects.
objectives: Understand and apply Python environment & foundations in Python.
Explain how Python versions changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Python versions with installation and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
examples:
import sys, keyword
name = "Ahmed"
print(sys.version_info.major)
print(type(name))
print(keyword.iskeyword("class"))

student_name = "Ahmed"
MAX_RETRIES = 3
print(student_name, MAX_RETRIES)

text = "python"
print([name for name in dir(text) if name.startswith("is")][:6])

import os
mode = os.environ.get("APP_MODE", "development")
print(mode)
print(str.upper.__doc__.splitlines()[0])
commonMistakes: Treating variable names as fixed-type boxes.
lessons.explain: Before syntax becomes useful, you need a reliable workflow: know which Python version is running, how a .py file is executed, how the command line and editor fit together, how environment variables affect programs, and how help() and dir() let you inspect unfamiliar objects.

lessons.title: Variables & types
lessons.explain: A variable is a name bound to a value. Python is dynamically typed — you don't declare the type, it's inferred.
lessons.example:
age = 21
name = "Ahmed"
print(f"{name} is {age}")
objectives: Bind values to names and recognize Python's core built-in types
Use valid, descriptive Python names and explain dynamic name binding
Explain how dynamic typing changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect dynamic typing with f-strings and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Assuming a variable's type is fixed once assigned -- Python lets the same name later be rebound to a completely different type.
lessons.explanation: A variable is a name bound to a value. Python is dynamically typed — you don't declare the type, it's inferred.
examples:
age = 21
name = "Ahmed"

lessons.title: Basic syntax, strings, formatting & conversion
objectives: Format, slice, join, and convert strings
Read basic Python syntax and safely convert user input
Explain how f-string changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect f-string with f" and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Python uses indentation to define blocks and # for comments. Strings are immutable sequences.
examples:
# A comment explains intent
course = "Python"
hours = 20
print(course, hours)

text = "Python Programming"
print(text.upper())
print(text[:6])
print(text[-11:])

name = "Ahmed"
score = 92
print("{} scored {}".format(name, score))

raw = "21"
age = int(raw)
print(age + 1)
print(float(age))

name = "Ahmed"  # imagine this came from input()
print("Welcome,", name)

name = 'Ada'
print(f"{name} is great")     # Ada is great
s = 'hello'
print(s[1:4])                  # 'ell'
print(', '.join(['a','b','c'])) # 'a, b, c'
print(int("5") + 3)            # 8
commonMistakes: Forgetting a slice's end index is exclusive (s[1:4] gives 3 characters, not 4), or trying to add a string and number directly without converting first.
lessons.careerRelevance: f-strings, slicing, and explicit conversion are used constantly in real formatting and parsing code.

lessons.title: Conditionals, boolean logic & operators
lessons.explain: Conditionals choose which code runs. if/elif/else combines comparisons with boolean logic.
objectives: Write clear if/elif/else branches
Combine comparisons with boolean logic
Recognize when bitwise operators are appropriate
commonMistakes: Writing a while loop whose condition never becomes false, causing an infinite loop.

examples:
READ = 0b001
WRITE = 0b010

lessons.title: Loops in depth: for, while, break, continue & enumerate
objectives: Choose between for and while loops
Control loops safely with break and continue
Use enumerate() instead of a manual index when appropriate
lessons.explanation: Loops repeat work. A for loop is best for iterating through a sequence or range; a while loop is useful when repetition depends on a changing condition.
examples:
attempts = 3
while attempts > 0:
    print("attempts left:", attempts)
    attempts -= 1
print("done")

total = 0
for value in [2, 4, 6]:
    total += value
print(total)
commonMistakes: Using a while loop whose condition never becomes false (forgetting to update the loop variable), causing an infinite loop.
lessons.careerRelevance: Correctly choosing and controlling loops, and using enumerate(), signals real day-to-day Python fluency.
lessons.explain: Loops repeat work. A for loop is best for iterating through a sequence or range; a while loop is useful when repetition depends on a changing condition.

lessons.title: Lists, tuples, sets & sorting
objectives: Choose between lists, tuples, and sets
Build and transform collections
Sort without confusing in-place and returned results
lessons.explanation: Python's core collections serve different jobs. Lists are ordered and mutable, tuples are ordered and immutable, and sets store unique values with fast membership checks.
examples:
names = ['Zara', 'Ali', 'Mona']
print(sorted(names))
print(names)  # original list is unchanged

tags = {'python', 'git', 'python'}
print(tags)
coords = (25.2, 55.3)
print(coords[0])

nums = [1,2,3]
print(len(nums))       # 3
nums.append(4)         # nums is now [1,2,3,4]
doubled = [x*2 for x in range(3)]  # [0,2,4]
commonMistakes: Confusing a list comprehension's iteration order — [x*2 for x in range(3)] iterates 0,1,2, giving [0,2,4], not starting from 1.
lessons.careerRelevance: List comprehensions are idiomatic Python — real codebases and interviews both expect comfort reading and writing them.
lessons.explain: Python's core collections serve different jobs. Lists are ordered and mutable, tuples are ordered and immutable, and sets store unique values with fast membership checks.
lessons.example:

print(names)  # original list is unchanged

lessons.title: Mutability, identity & copying
objectives: Explain mutation and aliasing
Distinguish equality from identity
Choose shallow or deep copying intentionally
lessons.explanation: Lists and dictionaries are mutable, while strings and tuples are immutable. == compares values; is compares object identity.
examples:
import copy
original = {'items': [['A'], ['B']]}
shallow = copy.copy(original)
deep = copy.deepcopy(original)
original['items'][0].append('changed')
print(shallow['items'][0])  # shares nested list
print(deep['items'][0])     # independent

a = [1,2,3]
b = a          # b refers to the SAME list object
b.append(4)
print(a)        # [1,2,3,4] -- a changed too

t = (1,2,3)     # tuple: immutable

print(type(5/2))   # <class 'float'> -- / always gives a float
print(type(5//2))  # <class 'int'> -- // (floor division) gives an int when both inputs are ints
commonMistakes: Assuming `b = a` creates an independent copy of a mutable object — it doesn't; both names point to the same list.
lessons.careerRelevance: This distinction directly explains a whole category of confusing bugs involving shared, unexpectedly-mutated data.
lessons.explain: Lists and dictionaries are mutable, while strings and tuples are immutable. == compares values; is compares object identity.

lessons.title: Dictionaries: creation & membership
objectives: Create and update dictionaries
Check or retrieve optional keys safely
Use a dictionary for lookup/counting tasks
lessons.explanation: A dictionary maps unique keys to values. Use key in d when you only need to test existence and d.get(key, default) when a missing key should produce a fallback.
examples:
d = dict()          # {}
d['name'] = 'Ada'
print('name' in d)   # True
print('age' in d)    # False -- no error raised
commonMistakes: Accessing a missing key directly (d['age']) instead of checking with `in` or using .get() first — this raises a KeyError.
lessons.careerRelevance: Safe key-checking is a small habit that prevents a very common runtime crash in real programs.
lessons.explain: A dictionary maps unique keys to values. Use key in d when you only need to test existence and d.get(key, default) when a missing key should produce a fallback.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.explain: Functions package one responsibility behind a name. Parameters receive inputs and return sends a reusable value back to the caller.
objectives: Define reusable functions
Use parameters and return values
Explain the difference between returning and printing
commonMistakes: Expecting a variable assigned inside a function to be visible outside it, without an explicit return.
lessons.explanation: Functions package one responsibility behind a name. Parameters receive inputs and return sends a reusable value back to the caller.
examples:
def area(width, height):
    """Return rectangle area."""
    return width * height

print(area(4, 3))
print(area.__doc__)

lessons.title: Function arguments in depth
objectives: Design flexible function signatures
Use *args and **kwargs appropriately
Avoid mutable default argument bugs
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: recursion.
lessons.explanation: Function signatures describe how callers provide data. Default arguments make parameters optional, keyword arguments improve readability, *args gathers extra positional arguments, **kwargs gathers extra named arguments, and docstrings document the contract.
examples:
def greet(name, greeting="Hello"):
    return f"{greeting}, {name}"

print(greet("Ahmed"))
print(greet(name="Ahmed", greeting="Welcome"))

def report(scores, *tags, **meta):
    print(sum(scores) / len(scores))
    print(tags)
    print(meta)

report([80,90,100], "DSA", level="beginner")
commonMistakes: Using a mutable default argument like def f(x=[]) — the same list object is reused across calls that don't pass x.
lessons.careerRelevance: Flexible function signatures (*args/**kwargs) are common in real library code you'll write and read. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.
lessons.explain: Function signatures describe how callers provide data. Default arguments make parameters optional, keyword arguments improve readability, *args gathers extra positional arguments, **kwargs gathers extra named arguments, and docstrings document the contract.

lessons.title: Variable scope & None
objectives: Predict which binding a name refers to
Use None to represent an absent result
Explain how local scope changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect local scope with enclosing scope and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Scope determines where a name can be resolved. Function-local names normally stay inside the function; enclosing and global scopes are searched when a name is not local.
examples:
def f():
    x = 5
    return x
print(f())     # 5
# print(x)     # NameError -- x doesn't exist out here
result = None  # explicitly 'no value yet'
commonMistakes: Expecting a variable assigned inside a function to be accessible outside it without being returned — it isn't, by default.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding scope prevents a very common category of 'variable not defined' confusion.
lessons.explain: Scope determines where a name can be resolved. Function-local names normally stay inside the function; enclosing and global scopes are searched when a name is not local.
lessons.example:
def f():
    x = 5
    return x
print(f())     # 5
# print(x)     # NameError -- x doesn't exist out here
result = None  # explicitly 'no value yet'

lessons.title: First-class functions, lambda & closures
objectives: Pass functions as values
Use lambda for small expressions
Explain how a closure remembers enclosing state
lessons.explanation: Python functions are first-class objects: they can be stored, passed to other functions, and returned. A lambda is a compact anonymous function for a small expression.
lessons.explain: Python functions are first-class objects: they can be stored, passed to other functions, and returned. A lambda is a compact anonymous function for a small expression.
examples:
records = [('A', 3), ('B', 1), ('C', 2)]
print(sorted(records, key=lambda item: item[1]))
commonMistakes: Using lambda for multi-step logic makes code harder to read; use a named function when the behavior needs explanation or multiple statements.

lessons.title: Aptech Beginner 6 — Modules & the standard library
lessons.explanation: Modules organize reusable Python code. You can import your own files or standard-library modules, inspect available names with dir(), and choose clear import styles so dependencies stay readable.
objectives: Organize code into modules and use common standard-library modules confidently.
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: virtual environments (venv), dependency isolation.
Explain how modules changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect modules with import and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
examples:
import math
print(math.sqrt(81))
print(math.pi)

import sys
print(sys.version_info.major)
print(len(sys.argv))

from math import ceil, floor
print(ceil(3.2), floor(3.8))

import time
start = time.perf_counter()
sum(range(10000))
print(time.perf_counter() - start)

import math
public_names = [name for name in dir(math) if not name.startswith('_')]
print(public_names[:8])
commonMistakes: Naming your own file math.py or time.py can shadow the standard-library module you intended to import.
lessons.explain: Modules organize reusable Python code. You can import your own files or standard-library modules, inspect available names with dir(), and choose clear import styles so dependencies stay readable.
lessons.careerRelevance: These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.
lessons.example:
import math
print(math.sqrt(81))
print(math.pi)

lessons.title: Exceptions, raise & custom errors
objectives: Catch expected exceptions narrowly
Use else/finally correctly
Raise and define a simple custom exception
lessons.explanation: Exceptions represent runtime failures that normal control flow cannot complete. Catch only errors you can handle meaningfully, use else for work that depends on the try block succeeding, finally for cleanup that must run, and raise when your own function must reject invalid input.
examples:
resource = 'open'
try:
    print('using resource')
finally:
    resource = 'closed'
print(resource)
commonMistakes: Catching every possible exception with a bare `except:` instead of the specific one expected — this can hide real, unrelated bugs.
lessons.careerRelevance: Graceful error handling separates a robust program from one that crashes on the first bad input.
lessons.explain: Exceptions represent runtime failures that normal control flow cannot complete. Catch only errors you can handle meaningfully, use else for work that depends on the try block succeeding, finally for cleanup that must run, and raise when your own function must reject invalid input.

lessons.title: Files, directories & safe serialization
objectives: Read and write files safely
Work with paths and directories using pathlib
Explain why pickle must not load untrusted data
lessons.explanation: Use with open(..) so files close reliably even if an error occurs. Choose read/write/append modes deliberately, use pathlib for paths and directory operations, and handle expected I/O failures.
examples:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('notes.txt')
p.write_text('First note\nSecond note', encoding='utf-8')
with p.open(encoding='utf-8') as f:
    contents = f.read()
print(contents)
p.unlink()

from io import StringIO
stream = StringIO()
stream.write('hello')
stream.seek(0)
print(stream.read())

from pathlib import Path
p = Path('example.txt')
p.write_text('alpha\nbeta', encoding='utf-8')
print(p.read_text(encoding='utf-8'))
p.unlink()

from pathlib import Path
p = Path('.')
print(p.exists(), p.is_dir())

import pickle
data = {'scores': [10, 20]}
blob = pickle.dumps(data)
print(pickle.loads(blob))
commonMistakes: Opening a file without `with` (or a matching close()) — the file can remain open longer than intended.
lessons.careerRelevance: Safe file handling is a baseline expectation in any real, non-toy Python script.
lessons.explain: Use with open(..) so files close reliably even if an error occurs. Choose read/write/append modes deliberately, use pathlib for paths and directory operations, and handle expected I/O failures.
lessons.example:
from pathlib import Path
p = Path('notes.txt')
p.write_text('First note\nSecond note', encoding='utf-8')
with p.open(encoding='utf-8') as f:
    contents = f.read()
print(contents)
p.unlink()

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 1 — Classes, objects & special methods
lessons.explain: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance built from it. __init__ runs at creation; self refers to the specific object.
objectives: Define a class and create instances from it
Explain how class changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect class with __init__ and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Forgetting `self` as the first parameter of an instance method, or confusing the class (blueprint) with an object (instance).

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 2 — Encapsulation & valid state
objectives: Bundle data and behavior together, and control access to internal state
Explain how encapsulation changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect encapsulation with internal state and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Encapsulation means bundling data (attributes) and the methods that operate on it inside one class, while controlling what's exposed to the outside. A leading underscore (_balance) is Python's convention signaling 'internal, don't touch directly,' even though it's not strictly enforced.
commonMistakes: Exposing internal attributes directly and letting external code modify them freely, bypassing any validation the class's own methods would apply.
lessons.careerRelevance: Encapsulation is one of the four pillars of OOP and directly prevents a whole category of 'object got into an invalid state' bugs.
lessons.explain: Encapsulation means bundling data (attributes) and the methods that operate on it inside one class, while controlling what's exposed to the outside. A leading underscore (_balance) is Python's convention signaling 'internal, don't touch directly,' even though it's not strictly enforced.

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 3 — Abstraction
objectives: Expose only what's necessary, hiding implementation detail
Explain how abstraction changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect abstraction with abstract class and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Abstraction means exposing a simple interface while hiding the complex implementation behind it. When you call .sort() on a list, you don't need to know which sorting algorithm runs underneath -- that detail is abstracted away.
commonMistakes: Exposing every internal implementation detail through the public interface, forcing users of a class to understand its internals just to use it.
lessons.careerRelevance: Abstraction is what lets large codebases stay usable -- you can use a well-designed class without reading its internals.
lessons.explain: Abstraction means exposing a simple interface while hiding the complex implementation behind it. When you call .sort() on a list, you don't need to know which sorting algorithm runs underneath -- that detail is abstracted away.

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 4 — Inheritance & super()
lessons.explain: A subclass reuses a parent's code and overrides what differs. super() calls the parent's version.
objectives: Reuse and extend a parent class's behavior in a subclass
Explain how inheritance changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect inheritance with super() and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Overriding a method entirely when you meant to extend it -- forgetting to call super() loses the parent's behavior.
lessons.explanation: A subclass reuses a parent's code and overrides what differs. super() calls the parent's version.

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 5 — Polymorphism & duck typing
lessons.explain: Same method name, different behavior. Code calling .area() works for any shape without type checks.
lessons.example: total = sum(s.area() for s in shapes)
objectives: Write code that works with any object implementing the expected interface
Explain how polymorphism changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect polymorphism with duck typing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
commonMistakes: Adding explicit type-checks (isinstance chains) instead of relying on polymorphism to handle each type correctly.

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 6 — Composition vs inheritance
objectives: Choose between 'is-a' inheritance and 'has-a' composition
Explain how composition changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect composition with is-a and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship (a Dog IS-A Animal). Composition models a 'has-a' relationship (a Car HAS-A Engine) by holding an instance of another class as an attribute, rather than inheriting from it.
commonMistakes: Reaching for inheritance by default for every kind of code reuse, even when the relationship is really 'has-a' rather than 'is-a.'
lessons.careerRelevance: "Favor composition over inheritance" is one of the most repeated, real pieces of OOP design advice in professional codebases.
lessons.explain: Inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship (a Dog IS-A Animal). Composition models a 'has-a' relationship (a Car HAS-A Engine) by holding an instance of another class as an attribute, rather than inheriting from it.

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 7 — Interfaces & abstract base classes
objectives: Use abstract classes to enforce a shared contract across subclasses
Explain how abstract class changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect abstract class with contract and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: An abstract class defines a contract -- methods every subclass MUST implement -- without providing (or only partially providing) the implementation itself. This lets you write code that works with ANY subclass polymorphically, as long as it fulfills the contract, without needing to know which specific subclass it is at runtime.
commonMistakes: Trying to instantiate an abstract class directly -- it's meant to be subclassed, not used on its own, and most languages enforce this.
lessons.careerRelevance: Programming against an interface/abstract contract, not a concrete class, is a foundational skill for writing flexible, testable code.
lessons.explain: An abstract class defines a contract -- methods every subclass MUST implement -- without providing (or only partially providing) the implementation itself. This lets you write code that works with ANY subclass polymorphically, as long as it fulfills the contract, without needing to know which specific subclass it is at runtime.

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 8 — SOLID principles
objectives: Recognize each of the five SOLID principles
Explain how SOLID changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect SOLID with single responsibility and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: SOLID is five design principles: Single Responsibility (a class should have one reason to change), Open/Closed (open for extension, closed for modification -- add new behavior without editing existing code), Liskov Substitution (a subclass should be usable anywhere its parent class is expected, without breaking things).
examples:
# Single Responsibility violated: a class that both saves to a database
# AND formats a report AND sends an email -- three reasons to change

# Dependency Inversion: a function that depends on an abstract 'Notifier'
# interface, not a concrete 'EmailSender' class directly -- swap implementations freely
commonMistakes: Treating SOLID as rigid rules to follow everywhere regardless of context, rather than principles that guide judgment about trade-offs.
lessons.careerRelevance: SOLID vocabulary is widely used in real code reviews and design discussions -- recognizing the terms is expected of an experienced engineer.
lessons.explain: SOLID is five design principles: Single Responsibility (a class should have one reason to change), Open/Closed (open for extension, closed for modification -- add new behavior without editing existing code), Liskov Substitution (a subclass should be usable anywhere its parent class is expected, without breaking things).

lessons.title: Aptech OOP 9 — Design patterns & design judgment
objectives: Recognize a few common design patterns and what problem each solves
Explain how design pattern changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect design pattern with singleton and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A design pattern is a reusable, named solution to a recurring design problem. Singleton ensures a class has only one instance globally.
commonMistakes: Forcing a design pattern into code where it doesn't actually fit, just because it's a known pattern -- patterns solve specific problems, they're not universally 'better.'
lessons.careerRelevance: Recognizing common design patterns by name is a frequent, practical interview and code-review topic.
lessons.explain: A design pattern is a reusable, named solution to a recurring design problem. Singleton ensures a class has only one instance globally.

lessons.title: Aptech Beginner 10 — Regular expressions
lessons.explanation: Regular expressions describe text patterns. Learn literal and special characters, character classes, quantifiers, grouping, anchors, match objects, substitution, splitting, compilation and flags.
objectives: Build and explain practical regular expressions using Python re.
Explain how re changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect re with character classes and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
examples:
import re
print(bool(re.fullmatch(r'[A-Za-z]+', 'Python')))

import re
m = re.search(r'(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})', 'Date: 2026-08-13')
print(m.groups())

import re
print(re.sub(r'\s+', '-', 'data structures and algorithms'))

import re
print(re.split(r'[,;]\s*', 'python, dsa; sql'))

import re
pattern = re.compile(r'^python$', re.IGNORECASE)
print(bool(pattern.match('PYTHON')))
commonMistakes: A greedy quantifier can consume more text than you intended; tighten the pattern or use a non-greedy quantifier when appropriate.
lessons.explain: Regular expressions describe text patterns. Learn literal and special characters, character classes, quantifiers, grouping, anchors, match objects, substitution, splitting, compilation and flags.

lessons.title: Iterators & generators
objectives: Understand the iterator protocol and write memory-efficient generators with yield
Explain how iter() changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect iter() with next() and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: An iterator produces one value at a time instead of building every result up front. Python for-loops use the iterator protocol internally: iter(obj) gets an iterator and next(iterator) requests the next item until StopIteration.
commonMistakes: Converting a generator to list immediately removes its memory advantage.
lessons.careerRelevance: This topic appears in modern software/backend internship requirements or technical interviews and strengthens transferable engineering fundamentals.
lessons.explanation: An iterator produces one value at a time instead of building every result up front. Python for-loops use the iterator protocol internally: iter(obj) gets an iterator and next(iterator) requests the next item until StopIteration.

lessons.title: Decorators: wrapping behavior cleanly
objectives: Write and apply function decorators while preserving the wrapped function
Explain how decorator changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect decorator with closure and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: A decorator takes a function and returns a new function that adds behavior around it. This pattern is common in Python frameworks for authentication, logging, caching, retries, routing, and tests.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to return the wrapper from the decorator, or forgetting to return the wrapped function result from the wrapper.

lessons.title: Context managers & resource safety
objectives: Use with statements and create a custom context manager for reliable cleanup
Explain how with changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect with with __enter__ and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: A context manager defines setup and cleanup around a block of work. The with statement guarantees cleanup even when an exception occurs, which is why files, locks, database connections, and transactions often use it.
commonMistakes: Doing cleanup after the with block manually defeats the safety benefit.

lessons.title: Python concurrency: threads, asyncio, locks & race conditions
objectives: Explain Python concurrency choices and protect shared state with a lock
Explain how threading changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect threading with asyncio and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Concurrency lets tasks make progress during the same time period. Threads are useful for many blocking I/O workloads, asyncio coordinates many I/O tasks cooperatively, and processes are often preferred for CPU-heavy parallel work.
lessons.example:
from threading import Lock

balance = 100
lock = Lock()

def withdraw(amount):
    global balance
    with lock:
        if balance >= amount:
            balance -= amount
            return True
        return False

print(withdraw(30), balance)
commonMistakes: Assuming the GIL makes shared-state logic automatically safe.

lessons.title: Decimal & money-safe arithmetic
objectives: Represent monetary values without binary floating-point surprises
Explain how Decimal changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect Decimal with integer cents and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explain: Financial code should avoid using binary floating point for money because values such as 0.1 cannot be represented exactly. Two common approaches are Decimal constructed from strings, or storing the smallest currency unit as an integer (for example cents).
lessons.example:
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

price = Decimal("19.99")
tax = Decimal("0.05")
total = (price * (Decimal("1") + tax)).quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
print(total)

amount_cents = 1999
print(amount_cents + 501)
commonMistakes: Creating Decimal from a float, such as Decimal(0.1), imports the float approximation.

exercises.hint: overriding __init__ in a subclass completely replaces the parent's __init__ unless you explicitly call super().__init__(...) -- without it, none of the parent class's setup runs, so any attributes or state the parent was responsible for initializing simply don't exist

deliverables: A 'before' version with at least 2 genuine design problems (e.g. a class violating single responsibility, inheritance misused where composition fits better)

projects.portfolioTips: The 'before' and 'after' together, with a clear explanation of what each change actually fixes, is far more convincing than a clean greenfield design -- it's direct evidence you can improve real code under real constraints, which is most of what actual engineering work looks like.
projects.desc: Take a small system that technically works but has real design problems (a class doing too many unrelated things, inheritance used where composition would fit better, hardcoded dependencies that make testing hard) and refactor it applying SOLID principles deliberately -- not just because a checklist says to, but because you can explain what specific problem each change fixes. This capstone is about design judgment under a realistic 'this already works, don't break it' constraint, not designing a clean system from a blank page.

description: The foundation everything else is built on — syntax through advanced features.

interviewPreparation.q: Why is using a mutable default argument (like `def f(x=[])`) considered a common Python bug?
interviewPreparation.a: Default argument values are evaluated once, when the function is defined, not fresh on every call. A mutable default (like a list) is shared across every call that doesn't explicitly pass their own -- mutations from one call silently leak into the next. The fix is to default to None and create a new mutable object inside the function body when it's None.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between a list and a generator, and when would you choose one over the other?
interviewPreparation.a: A list holds all its items in memory at once; a generator produces items lazily, one at a time, computing each only when requested. For large or unbounded sequences, a generator avoids loading everything into memory -- at the cost of only being iterable once, unlike a list you can loop over repeatedly.

interviewPreparation.q: What is the GIL (Global Interpreter Lock), and why does it matter for concurrency in Python?
interviewPreparation.a: The GIL ensures only one thread executes Python bytecode at a time in the standard CPython interpreter, which means CPU-bound multi-threaded code doesn't get real parallelism from threads alone. For CPU-bound work, multiprocessing (separate processes, each with its own GIL) is the common workaround; for I/O-bound work, threading still helps since the GIL is released during I/O waits.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you structure a Python project so it's genuinely maintainable and testable?
interviewPreparation.a: Separate concerns into modules with clear responsibilities, keep business logic separate from I/O/side effects so it's testable in isolation, use a proper package layout with a pyproject.toml, write tests that cover real behavior (not just imports succeeding), and avoid tightly coupling code to a specific execution context so it can be reused and tested independently.

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between `is` and `==` in Python, and why does this trip people up?
interviewPreparation.a: `==` checks value equality (are these two things equal in content); `is` checks identity (are these the literal same object in memory). Small integers and short strings are sometimes cached by CPython and happen to pass an `is` check that wouldn't hold for larger values, which misleads people into thinking `is` checks values -- it doesn't, and using `is` for value comparison is a real, if subtle, bug.

A test suite (pytest) covering the tool's core logic, not just a smoke test
Command-line argument handling (argparse or click) with a helpful --help output
A README documenting installation, usage, and at least one real example run
Basic error handling for at least one realistic failure case (bad input, missing file, network error)
